title: pair and tuple
learningGoals: return two values from a function

youtube.title: C++ std::pair and std::tuple | C++ Programming EP 71
youtube.description: In this episode you will use std pair, return two values from a function and unpack with structured bindings, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 pair and tuple · 0:46 A pair · 1:26 Parts of a pair · 1:56 Second program · 2:56 Recap · 3:26 Bug of the Day · 4:14 Challenge · 4:34 Next episode

thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to two shoes tied together, and a bundle of three

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we meet small bundles. A pair holds two values, a tuple holds more, and both are handy.

scenes.onScreen: "pair and tuple": numbered lines (1. A pair holds exactly two values; 2. A tuple holds any fixed number; 3. Structured bindings unpack them) and an analogy card: a pair of shoes, and a school bag with a few fixed items
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A pair holds two values, called first and second. A tuple holds any fixed number of values of any types. Both live in the standard library. Since C plus plus seventeen, you can unpack them in one line with structured bindings. Think of a pair of shoes. Two items, always together.
points: A pair holds exactly two values
A tuple holds any fixed number

analogy.title: pair and tuple
analogy.body: A pair of shoes, and a school bag with a few fixed items

scenes.onScreen: pair.cpp: a function returns the smallest and biggest in one pair
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The function returns a pair of ints. [HL 6] Make pair builds a pair from two values. [HL 10] The result goes in p. [HL 11] First is four, and second is nine. [HL 12] Square brackets after auto unpack the pair into two new names. [HL 13] Lo is two, and hi is seven.

scenes.onScreen: a table: the pair and its two members
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Here is the pair p. First is four, and second is nine. With a structured binding, you give the two parts their own names. That makes the code easier to read.

diagram.caption: a table: the pair and its two members

scenes.onScreen: tuple.cpp: a tuple holds a name, a mark and a pass flag
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 7] A tuple can hold values of different types. This one holds a string, an int and a bool. [HL 8] Get with an index in angle brackets reads one part. Index zero is the name. [HL 9] A structured binding unpacks all three parts. [HL 10] The output is Asha, ninety-one, true.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as tuple dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints Asha, and then Asha ninety-one true.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A pair holds two values. Two. A tuple holds any fixed number of values. Three. Use first and second for a pair. Four. Structured bindings unpack a pair or a tuple. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A tuple holds any fixed number of values.
Use first and second for a pair.
Structured bindings unpack a pair or a tuple.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A member that does not exist
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We ask a pair for its third member. The compiler says the pair has no member named third. A pair holds exactly two values. For three, use a tuple, or write a small struct.

scenes.onScreen: Two values walked into a pair. They said, we are a perfect match, first and second.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Two values walked into a pair. They said, we are a perfect match, first and second.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: return the quotient and the remainder
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a function that returns the quotient and the remainder of two ints as a pair. Print both. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: std map. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

pair.cpp: In function 'int main()':
pair.cpp:7:15: error: 'struct std::pair<int, int>' has no member named 'third'
    7 |     cout << p.third << endl;
      |               ^~~~~
bug.why: A pair has only first and second. For three or more values, use a tuple, or better, write a small struct with clear names.

pun: "Two values walked into a pair. They said, we are a perfect match, first and second."
challenge: Write a function that returns the quotient and the remainder of two ints as a pair. Print both.
challengeAnswer: Return make pair of a divided by b, and a remainder b. In main, print first and second.
